concepts.title: Lagrange Multipliers
concepts.text:
If you are constrained to some domain, how can you optimize a function?

g(x), the constraint, domain which you are allowed to be on.

$\nabla g$, normal to the constraint surface

f(x), the function you want to optimize

f(x) = C, the level curves

$\nabla f$, normal to the level curves of f. Since if $\vec v$ is along level curve, f constant $\nabla f \cdot v = 0$

$\frac{d}{dt} f(c(t)) = 0$ by def
$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\frac{dx_i}{dt} = 0 \Rightarrow \nabla f \cdot v = 0$

Intuition: imaging moving up the level curves. At some point, the curves will be "kissing", have a tangent line to, the constrained domain. the goal is to find these points. Having a tangent = $\nabla f \| \nabla g$ since $\nabla f \perp$ level curves. Therefore,

$\nabla f(x) + \lambda \nabla g(x) = 0$   w/   $g(x) = 0$
concepts.context: Diagram to the left shows $\nabla g$ and $\nabla f$ vectors normal to the constraint curve and level curves at their point of tangency.

A way to make the vector aware of its position

Pizza eats monkey vs Monkey eats pizza. Currently, the vectors are not position aware

- A simple idea could just be to concat a number to the end of the vector to denote the position.

- Instead we can add
  - A desirable property is regardless of n, the number of tokens, we want each position to represent the same vector

d×n   d×n   d×n
$X_{ij}^{(1)} = X_{ij}^{(0)} + P_{ij}$

Pizza Pos 1        Pizza        First word
$\begin{bmatrix}2.8\\3.9\\-1.2\\6\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\3\\-1\\5\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}0.8\\0.9\\-0.2\\1\end{bmatrix}$

$P_{ij} = \begin{cases}\sin\left(\frac{j}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) & i\ even\\ \cos\left(\frac{j}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) & i\ odd\end{cases}$

Why should this work better than just concat? What happens if we apply a linear trans. to the concat.?

$V\begin{bmatrix}X_i^{(0)}\\P_j\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}v_{11} & v_{12}\\v_{21} & v_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}X_i^{(0)}\\P_j\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}v_{11}X_i^{(0)} + v_{12}P_j\\v_{21}X_i^{(0)} + v_{22}P_j\end{bmatrix}$

$= \begin{bmatrix}v_{11}X_i^{(0)}\\v_{21}X_i^{(0)}\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}v_{12}P_j\\v_{22}P_j\end{bmatrix} = X_i^{(0)'} + P_j'$

concepts.title: Bisection Method / Binary Search
concepts.text:
Applys for cont. funcs. for which we know values w/ opposite signs. Pretty slow.

Basic idea: consider $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$. Guess two points a, b w/ $sgn(f(a)) \neq sgn(f(b))$.

$c = \frac{a+b}{2}$
Replace a or b w/ c → keeping the root

$|f(c)| < tol$ so we stop iteration and say that c is a root.

If evaluating on a fixed grid, worst case $O(\log n)$ function evals where n is grid size

concepts.title: Discrete Fourier transform
concepts.text:
Discrete Fourier transform

$\tilde{x}_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j e^{-2\pi i jk/n}$

$x_k = \sum \tilde{x}_j e^{i2\pi jk/n}$

$\mathcal{F}: \{x_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{C}} \to \{\tilde{x}_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{C}}$

amplitude vs time plot: $T_m$, $f_m$
$\tilde{x}_n$ vs Freq plot: $N/2$, $f_m$

Sample rate, each n = $t_s$, in which case in FD $\Delta f$ = 1Hz.

Parameters
- $f_s$ - sampling freq. tells you how many points to sample, the rate/max freq you can capture.
E.g. $f_s$ = 40k samples/sec → $f_{max}$ = 20kHz, $f_s/2$ is the Nyquist freq
- $\Delta t$ - sampling time, $\Delta t = 1/f_s$, spacing between time points
- N - Number of points in DFT $\{x_n\}_{n=0}^{N-1}$
- T - Duration of signal
- $\Delta f$ - spacing between freq bins, $\Delta f = 1/T$
e.g. 10s of data, $f_s$ = 1kHz, $\Delta f$ = 1/10 = 0.1Hz

Properties
Linearity: $\mathcal{F}(\{ax_n+by_n\})_k = aX_k+bY_k$
Rescaling: $\mathcal{F}(\{x_{n-a}\})_k = X_k \to \mathcal{F}(\{x_{n-a}\})\cdot X_{k-a}$
Loss: $\mathcal{F}(\{x_{2n}\})\cdot X_n \to \mathcal{F}(\{x_{2n}\})\cdot X_{n\pm N}$

DFT of Real Signals
If $x_n \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow X_k = X_{-k}^{*}$ (conjugate symmetric)
Since $\mathcal{F}$ is invertible, # independent components = N, known that $X_k \in \mathbb{C}$.

Fourier Uncertainty Principle

concepts.title: Batch Norm: $BN_{\gamma,\beta}(x_i)$
concepts.text:
Let L be some batch B with len M. Batch norm: $BN_{\gamma,\beta}(x_i)$
Say there are L batches and $x_i \in B$, $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^N$

During Training
$\mu_L = \dfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} x_i$
$\sigma_L^2 = \dfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} (x_i - \mu_B)^2$

Consider a d dimensional input vector $x_i^n \in B$   (dim: n, sample: i)
$\hat{x}_i^n = \dfrac{x_i^n - \mu_L^n}{\sqrt{(\sigma_L^n)^2 + \varepsilon}}$   w/ $\varepsilon \ll 1$
Makes sure no blowup if $\sigma \ll 1$

$y_i := \gamma \hat{x}_i + \beta$
w/o $\gamma, \beta$ the output would just be $N(0,1)$. So [we] reintroduce ability for [the network] to add variability.

Imagine in class, you tell everyone to speak [normalized] (norm.) to cut through noise. But then some people who have something important to say should say it. This is what $\gamma$ is [for].

Across all batches compute the "running avg"
$\mu_l = \rho \mu_{l-1} + (1-\rho)\mu_{B,l}$ where $l \in [0,L]$
$\sigma_l = \rho \sigma_{l-1} + (1-\rho)\sigma_{B,l-1}$   $\rho = 0.9$ is momentum

During Test
$\hat{x}_i^n = \dfrac{x_i^n - \mu_L^n}{\sqrt{(\sigma_L^n)^2+\varepsilon}}$
$y_i = \gamma\hat{x}_i + \beta$

If $\mu_L - \mu_R \gg 1$, then [the] test stat. is significantly [off]; the $\hat{x}_i^n$ aren't properly normalized
concepts.context: Derivation of Batch Normalization: per-batch mean/variance, the learnable scale/shift (gamma, beta), the running-average statistics used at test time, and a caution about train/test distribution mismatch.

concepts.title: Data-Reduction, Data-Driven FFT
concepts.text:
Data-Reduction, Data-Driven FFT   Guaranteed to exist & unique

goal is for transformation
. Find 2 vectors $v_1, u_1$ s.t. when transformed
$Av_1 \perp Au_1$. This translates to
finding 2 orthogonal matrices U,V
s.t. $A = U\Sigma V^T$

$v_1 \perp v_2$   unit vectors   $u_1 \perp u_2$
$Av_1 = \sigma_1 u_1$
$Av_2 = \sigma_2 u_2$
$A[v_1\, v_2] = [u_1\, u_2]\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_1 & 0\\ 0 & \sigma_2\end{bmatrix}$   Best orthogonalize $U^TU = I$
$AV = U\Sigma \rightarrow A = U\Sigma V^T$   Diagonal Matrix

$A^TA = V\Sigma^2 V^T$   Eigenvalues of $A^TA$
: the columns are eigenvectors of $A^TA$
$AA^T = U\Sigma^2 U^T$

$A = \left[\, | \; | \; \cdots \; | \,\right]$, $u_1, u_2, ..., u_n$, $k \in \mathbb{R}^n$

N x M matrix: $v_1, \sigma_1, ..., \sigma_m$ / 0 / eigenvectors
in the eigenbasis, $\sigma_1$ more important than $u_2$... each $u_i$ can be expanded w/ basis of $u_1, u_2$. Basis for column space of A.
Right singular vectors, basis for row space of A

Example: Say [you] have many signals f(t) vs freq and you want to break down into vectors which describe the ensemble of these signals, but you don't want to store all the signals. Then create $A = [f_1, ..., f_n]$ (matrix w/ n being number of signals). How can you only have a size q matrix to represent A w/o losing too much? [We] get the SVD: $A = \sigma_1\begin{bmatrix}u_1\\1\end{bmatrix}[-v_1-] + \sigma_2\begin{bmatrix}u_2\\1\end{bmatrix}[-v_2-] + ...$
$= \sum_i \sigma_i u_i v_i^T$
Since these are ordered by $\sigma_i$, you can take the first q and be good   Properties
Here $V^T$ shape $=$ q freq bins x q.

Now let's say you have a new signal, if it's similar to the others, you can put it in the $v_1...v_n$ basis by multiplying by $V^T$. You can also decompose vectors in the $v_1...v_n$ basis by multiplying by V.
concepts.context: Derivation of the Singular Value Decomposition (A = U Sigma V^T) and its use as a data-driven, data-reduction alternative to the FFT for representing an ensemble of signals.

concepts.title: Nyquist Frequency
concepts.text:
Nyquist Frequency
How to properly digitize a signal?

A function, g, containing no frequency > W Hz is completely determined by sampling @ 2W Hz. That is if you want to perfectly capture information of g, you need to sample @ 2W.
we care about W freq, $\Delta t_{sample} = \dfrac{1}{2W}$

Interesting point: if you randomly sample a simple high freq signal you can on average beat Shannon Nyquist theorem!

Proof:
Supp. x(t) is bandlimited X(f); $\mathcal{F}(x(t)) = 0$ for $f > f_{max}$.
The sampled signal $x_s(t) = x(t)\, \text{III}_{\Delta t}(t)$ where $\Delta t = 1/f_s$ and
$\text{III}_{\Delta t}(t) := \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - n\Delta t)$ is the dirac comb $\rightarrow$ (comb of spikes)
$X_s(f) = \mathcal{F}[x_s(t)](f) = \mathcal{F}[x(t)\, \text{III}_{\Delta t}(t)] = \mathcal{F}[x(t)] * \mathcal{F}[\text{III}_{\Delta t}(t)]$

concepts.title: Fast Convolutions
concepts.text:
Fast Convolutions
Algorithm: find $a * b$

$a = [a_0, a_1, ... a_{n-1}]$
$f(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + ... a_{n-1}x^{n-1}$   write as poly.

$b = [b_0, b_1, ... b_{n-1}]$
$g(x) = b_0 + b_1 x + ... b_{n-1}x^{n-1}$

FFT $\rightarrow$   $\hat{a} = [\hat{a}_0, \hat{a}_1, ... \hat{a}_{n-1}]$
FFT $\rightarrow$   $\hat{b} = [\hat{b}_0, \hat{b}_1, ... \hat{b}_{n-1}]$
Dot product $\downarrow$
$\hat{a}\cdot\hat{b} = [\hat{a}_0\hat{b}_0, \hat{a}_1\hat{b}_1, ...]$
Inv. FFT $\leftarrow$

$a*b = \left[ a_0b_0;\; a_0b_1+a_1b_0;\; a_0b_2+a_1b_1+a_2b_0;\; \vdots \right]$

Why does it work?
Convolution Theorem
$u*v = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[\mathcal{F}(u)\mathcal{F}(v)\right]$, $u,v \in L(\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R})$
(see pg. 133 scratch notes)
concepts.context: Algorithm for computing a convolution a*b quickly via FFT (multiply in frequency domain, then inverse FFT), justified by the convolution theorem.

    Minimizing KL divergence = to

when does the data go?

factored out all the $f(\Theta|d_i)$ terms since not func. of $\psi_i$

Monte Carlo   unbiased!

Estimate area of circle by throwing darts

[diagram: square containing a circle with scattered dots]

$= 2\int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{1-x^2}\, dx = \sum_i 2\sqrt{1-x_i^2}$

$x_i \sim Uniform(-1,1)$

generally very useful for integrals, especially high dimensional ones

e.g. Estimate $\int e^{-x} dx = \hat p$ and variance of MC.

$\hat p = E_{x\sim[0,1]}[e^{-x}] = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_i e^{-x_i}$, $x_i \sim [0,1]$

$\sigma = E_{x\sim[0,1]}[(e^{-x})^2] - E_{x\sim[0,1]}[e^{-x}]^2$ = can calculate exactly all integrals

e.g. Estimate $\int d\vec x\, N(x,1) f(\vec x) = \hat p$

$\hat p = E_{x\sim N(x,1)}[f(\vec x)]$

ML then follows ordinary statistics for example

$\hat p \pm 1.96 \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt N}$ is the 95% confidence interval for your integral.

Generally you don't know $\theta$ but can take all possible values <- True value

Nice Monte Carlo Properties

1). Consistent: $\lim_{n\to\infty} Pr(|\frac{1}{n}\sum x_i - \theta| > \epsilon) = 0$

2). Unbiased: $\hat\theta(\int dx\, p(x)) = E[p(x)] = \theta$

concepts.title: Metropolis - Hastings Algorithm
concepts.text:
Metropolis - Hastings Algorithm

Say you have prob. dist. P(x) ->

This algo will let you draw samples from P(x) if you know P(x) $\propto$ f(x)

Steps: $T(x_{t+1}|x_t)$

0. Initialization: choose $x_0$ starting point.
Choose $g(x'|y)$ <- Transition kernel / Random point / Proposal density. For example, this could be a simple gaussian $x \sim N(y,1)$

1). For t:
> Generate proposed point $x'$ by $g(x'|x_t)$
> Calc acc. ratio $\left[1, \dfrac{P(x')g(x_t|x')}{P(x_t)g(x'|x_t)}\right]$ <- so possible this is >1

In some ref. prob to accept x' -> u ~ Uniform[0,1]
if u < acc: accept $x_{t+1} = x'$
if u > acc: reject $x_{t+1} = x_t$

Markov Property
Irreducibility: True does N(non) have non-zero prob everywhere.
Aperiodic: True does P to the x' will not get accepted
$\therefore$ This markov chain converges to a unique stationary distribution

So if we prove $P(x_t)T(x_{t+1}|x_t) = P(x_{t+1})T(x_t|x_{t+1})\ \forall x$
=> The markov chain $\{\pi^t\}$ will converge to P(x)

Case 1: Rejection, $x_{t+1} = x_t$, denote
Case 2: Acceptance, $x_{t+1} = x'$

LHS: $P(x_t)T(x'|x_t) = P(x_t)g(x'|x_t)\min\left[1,\dfrac{P(x')g(x_t|x')}{P(x_t)g(x'|x_t)}\right]$

$= \min\left[P(x_t)g(x'|x_t),\ P(x')g(x_t|x')\right]$

RHS: $P(x')T(x_t|x') = P(x')g(x_t|x')\min\left[1,\dfrac{P(x_t)g(x'|x_t)}{P(x')g(x_t|x')}\right]$

$= \min\left[P(x')g(x_t|x'),\ P(x_t)g(x'|x_t)\right]$

$T(x_{t+1}=x'|x_t) = g(x'|x_t)\alpha(x_t,x')$

$T(x_{t+1}=x_t|x_t) = 1 - \int dx'\, g(x'|x_t)\alpha(x_t,x')$

Case: Prob. going to $x_t$ = 1 - Prob going to some $x'$

concepts.title: How to choose priors
concepts.text:
How to choose priors

pt 1: what is an uninformative prior

Coin flip $p(Heads) = \theta$.  Supp. $\theta \sim U[0,1]$

what is $p(2\ heads)$? It is $\theta^2 = \phi$

$p(\phi) = p(\theta)\dfrac{d\theta}{d\phi} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\phi}}$

[graph: $p(\theta)$ flat near 1 then drops to 0 at $\theta=1$]
[graph: $p(\phi)$ decreasing curve to 0 at $\phi=1$]

so even though we have an "uninformative prior" in $\theta$ we don't have an uninformative prior in $\theta^2$

Special case Jeffrey's prior

$p(\theta) = \sqrt{I(\theta)}$ . what happens if you change parametrization?

$p(\phi) = p(\theta)\dfrac{d\theta}{d\phi} = \sqrt{\dfrac{d\theta}{d\phi^2}}\dfrac{d\theta}{d\phi} = 1$ . So invariant!
concepts.context: Shows that a uniform (uninformative) prior is not invariant under reparametrization, motivating Jeffreys' prior which is.

concepts.title: Can an inconsistent biased estimator be more useful than a biased consistent one?
concepts.text:
Can an inconsistent biased estimator be more useful than a biased consistent one?

Supp. 1 sample from $p(x) = N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and want $\mu_x$

Estimator 1: $\hat\mu_x = \dfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i$

Estimator 2: $\hat{\hat\mu}_x = \alpha\hat\mu_x$ w/ $0<\alpha<1$

[graph: bell curve labeled "draw from p" with points $\mu_x$, $\hat{\hat\mu}_x$, $\hat\mu_x$ marked on the x-axis]

So an inconsistent biased estimator is better in the MSE = bias$^2$ + var sense. In particular

MLE $\hat\mu_x$: $0 + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{N}$

MLE $\hat{\hat\mu}_x$: $(\alpha\mu-\mu)^2 + \alpha^2\dfrac{\sigma^2}{N}$

So if $\sigma \gg 1$, or $N \sim 1$   $\hat{\hat\mu}$ has a better MSE!

concepts.title: Crammer Rao Bound
concepts.text:
Crammer Rao Bound
Sep. you have an estimator $\hat\theta$, and bias $b(\hat\theta)$ how would you find the lowest possible variance?
Assumptions:
1). $\forall \theta_1,\theta_2 \in \Theta$ st $\theta_1 \ne \theta_2$, $p(x|\theta_1) \ne p(x|\theta_2)$
2). $\{x\in X \mid f(x|\theta)>0\}$ doesn't dep. on θ eg $r(x|\theta)=U[0,\theta]$ violates this
3). Θ is open
4). $\exists\ \dfrac{\partial p(x|\theta)}{\partial\theta}$
5). $\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\dfrac{\partial \log p(x|\theta)}{\partial\theta}\big)^2\Big] < \infty$
Th. Let $x_1...x_n$ be random samples from $p(x|\theta)$ and supp. $\hat\theta$ is an estimator of θ. Then
$Var(\hat\theta) \ge \dfrac{(1+\partial b/\partial\theta)^2}{I_\theta}$ where $b(\theta) = bias(\hat\theta)$ $I_\theta = \mathbb{E}\big[(\partial\theta/\partial\theta)^2\big]$
concepts.context: Note misspells Cramér-Rao as 'Crammer Rao'; the final I_θ expression is written in tiny script and likely intends the Fisher information ∂log p(x|θ)/∂θ, matching assumption 5.

concepts.title: Savage - Dickey Ratio
concepts.text:
Savage - Dickey Ratio    Getting BF of Nested Models
If one has a nested model, e.g. $M_1(\Phi=\Phi_0)=M_2$ we can evaluate the Bayes factor between these models without explicitly integrating out the nuisance params.
as long as the priors are eq.
$p(\Phi|M_0) = p(\Phi|\Phi=\Phi_0,M_1)$
BF
$p(\Phi|d,M_1)$
$p(\Phi|M_1)$
Φ
see Wagenmakers et al. 2010 App. A
BF = $\dfrac{p(d|H_0)}{p(d|H_1)}$    Note $p(d|H_0) = \int p(d|\Phi,H_0)p(\Phi|H_0)d\Phi$ → $= \int p(d|\Phi,\Phi_0,H_1)p(\Phi|H_1)d\Phi$
assume $\lim_{\Phi\to\Phi_0} p(\Phi|\Phi_0,H_1) = p(\Phi|H_0)$ in the super model, the limit approaches the submodel
$= p(d|\Phi_0,H_1) = \dfrac{p(\Phi_0|d,H_1)\, p(d|H_1)}{p(\Phi_0|H_1)}$ Bayes rule

concepts.title: Self Information
concepts.text:
Self Information
why log? It's characteristic fcn.
Tells us the amount of information gained by observing
$I(x) = -\log_2 P(x)$
Why is this a good def.? Consider:
If you observe an unlikely event, $P(x)\sim 0 \Rightarrow I(x)\sim\infty$
If you observe a likely event, $P(x)\sim 1 \Rightarrow I(x)\sim 0$
E.g. consider you know the winning lottery ticket #, then you know about a very unlikely event and thus were told a lot of information. If you were told losing lottery numbers, then you aren't gaining much info. I mean, I could've told you that!

concepts.title: Nested Sampling
concepts.text:
Nested Sampling
A way to get the evidence $Z = p(d)$ and as a byproduct lets you sample from posterior.
Advantages:
1). Doesn't require initial guess
2). Samples from prior so technique can handle multimodality
3). Doesn't scale to high dimensions
$p(d) = \int d\Theta\, p(d|\Theta)p(\Theta)$
$= \int d\Theta\, L(\Theta)\pi(\Theta) = \lim_{\Delta\Theta\to0} \sum L(\Theta_i)\pi(\Theta_i)\Delta\Theta_i$
lets go from θ-likelihood which equal λ and you seek cumulative probability in λ or width λ
$\to \int L(x)\,dX(\lambda)$
likelihood corresponding to some equivalent      prior volume of iso-likelihood contours
$X = \int_{L(\theta)>\lambda} \pi(\theta)d\theta$
$Z \approx \sum L(\theta_1,\theta_2)\Delta\theta_1\Delta\theta_2$   $Z \approx \sum L(X)\Delta X$
the area under one
of volume 0.9 of
total (X(λ)) = 0.9 say
Why does it matter how you integrate?
If there are nice contours λ surfaces then better to integrate w/ dλ, if there are weird X surfaces
Algorithm
1. Sample n live points $\Theta_i \sim \pi(\Theta)$ and evaluate $L(\Theta_i)$
2). Remove $\Theta_i = \min L(\Theta_i)$. Call this $\Theta_i^*$ w/ $L(\Theta_i^*)$
3). Replace the point w/ $\Theta_2 \sim \pi(\Theta)$ s.t. $\int \pi(\Theta)d\Theta$ constrained if $L(\Theta) > L^*$; 0 if $L(\Theta) < L^*$
constrained prior
4). Repeat and we have estimate for $\{X_i, L(X_i)\}$, want to use them. Trapezoid rule!
$Z = \sum_i L_i^{()} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}[X_{n-1}(L_{n-1}) - X_{n+1}(L_{n+1})]$
Accumulate evidence $Z=\sum L\Delta X$
In practice you don't need X_n's precisely. Instead: estimator $t_i \sim Beta(N_{live},1)$. Why? Well, removing lowest likelihood point is like compressing w/ compression factor, since the point sampled randomly in the prior the dist. of compression for a live point $t_i = t$, i.e. $x_i = x_{i-1}\cdot t_i$, $t_i \sim Beta(N_{live},1)$, so we use that for the estimator.

concepts.title: Prior Volume of points
concepts.text:
Prior
Volume of points w/ $L(\theta)>\lambda$
$H(x) = \begin{cases}1, & x>0\\0, & x<0\end{cases}$ ← this being different...
$X(\lambda) = \int_\Theta \pi(\theta)\,H(L(\theta)-\lambda)\,d\theta \Rightarrow \dfrac{dX}{d\lambda} = \int_\Theta \pi(\theta)\,\delta(L(\theta)-\lambda)\,d\theta$
so then if λ are the possible likelihood values then
$Z = \displaystyle\int_0^1 X(\lambda)\,d\lambda = \int_0^1 \lambda(X)\dfrac{dX}{d\lambda}\,d\lambda = \int\int_\Theta \lambda(X)\,\pi(\theta)\,\delta(L(\theta)-\lambda)\,d\lambda\,d\theta$   $L(x)$
$= \int L(\theta)\pi(\theta)d(\theta) = \int L(X)dX$

concepts.text:
H - Hypothesis, HϵH - Point hypothesis, D. Data

H∈H, $y=10x+12$              H: $y=122x^{20}+...$              H: $y=10x^3-7x^2$
Crude MDL Principle
length = L(H) + L(D|H)
↑Length of Hypothesis   ↑Length of data given hypothesis
The best model of the data is the one which minimizes the length (minimizes compression)
Defining the length of the point hypothesis is arbitrary, how do you compute this in practice. Barron 1985. Instead use a new disc. of the process. Instead of encoding H encode 𝓗.
Refined MDL
stochastic complexity of D given 𝓗 = $L(D|\hat H) + COMP(\mathcal{H})$
$\hat H \in \mathcal{H}$ is the hypothesis which minimizes $L(D|H)$, $\forall H\in\mathcal{H}$.
So the new def. of data compression is given over the hypothesis not point hyp.
$L(\mathcal{H}) + \bar L(D|\mathcal{H})$
← Designed such that $\bar L(D|\mathcal{H})$ is small when $\exists H\in\mathcal{H}$ st $L(D|H)$ is small
"Universal codes"
